_provenance.notes: The Area M (Alaska Peninsula and Aleutian Islands) salmon fishery is one of the most controversial in Alaska because it intercepts sockeye salmon that would otherwise return to Bristol Bay — often called the 'intercept fishery.' Genetic Stock Identification shows that typically 50-75% of sockeye caught in Area M are Bristol Bay-origin fish bound for Nushagak, Egegik, or Naknek-Kvichak districts. This creates a fundamental allocation conflict between Area M seine fishermen and Bristol Bay drift gillnet permit holders.

policy_context.fundamental_conflict: Area M permit holders (Alaska Peninsula seine fishermen) vs. Bristol Bay drift gillnet fishermen. Both hold CFEC limited entry permits. Both catch the same fish. BB fishermen argue Area M intercepts reduce their sustainable yield.
policy_context.gsi_finding: GSI studies consistently show 60-70% of Area M sockeye are BB-origin fish. BB fishermen argue this represents 3-5 million fish/year taken from their fishery.
policy_context.area_m_counter: Area M permit holders argue they have equal rights to fish in their district. Their ancestors fished the same waters. The fish pass through Area M waters.
policy_context.current_management: Season timing restrictions and TAC limits in Area M were implemented in the late 1990s and 2000s to reduce intercept. Real-time GSI is used in some seasons to track stock composition.
policy_context.economic_stakes: Area M permits are worth $180,000-220,000 (2022 values). BB drift permits hit $248,000 in 2022. Total combined fishery represents $350-450M annually.
policy_context.bof_action_history: BOF has repeatedly considered but resisted full Area M closure, citing equal access rights under Alaska Constitution.
